title: Exploiting the complexity of Lattice Isomorphism Problem via Irreducible Decomposition
abstract:
The Lattice Isomorphism Problem (LIP) is a computational problem that has recently been introduced into cryptography and is believed to be hard. Its search version, Search Lattice Isomorphism Problem (SLIP), is considered even harder than the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP), yet its complexity is still not well understood. Haviv and Regev (SODA 2014) showed that the decisional version (DLIP) lies in a statistical zero-knowledge class and is therefore unlikely to be NP-hard. This result does not apply to the search version, which motivates the question of whether NP can reduce to SLIP.

Our main result answers this question negatively. We show that every language reducible to SLIP lies in AM and coAM, by analyzing the direct-sum structure of irreducible lattices. Consequently, NP cannot reduce to SLIP unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses, and there is no reduction from SVP to SLIP unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses.

We also study several problems closely related to LIP and establish reductions between its search, counting, and decisional variants. These connections mirror known relationships for graph isomorphism. Finally, we propose a new algorithm that uses a KZ basis to compute an orthogonal decomposition of a lattice.

      Abstract. The Lattice Isomorphism Problem (LIP) is a computational
      problem that has recently been introduced into cryptography and is be-
      lieved to be hard. Its search version, Search Lattice Isomorphism Prob-
      lem (SLIP), is considered even harder than the Shortest Vector Problem
      (SVP), yet its complexity is still not well understood. Haviv and Regev
      (SODA 2014) showed that the decisional version (DLIP) lies in a statis-
      tical zero-knowledge class and is therefore unlikely to be NP-hard. This
      result does not apply to the search version, which motivates the question
      of whether NP can reduce to SLIP.
      Our main result answers this question negatively. We show that every
      language reducible to SLIP lies in AM and coAM, by analyzing the direct-
      sum structure of irreducible lattices. Consequently, NP cannot reduce to
      SLIP unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses, and there is no reduction
      from SVP to SLIP unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses.
      We also study several problems closely related to LIP and establish re-
      ductions between its search, counting, and decisional variants. These con-
      nections mirror known relationships for graph isomorphism. Finally, we
      propose a new algorithm that uses a KZ basis to compute an orthogonal
      decomposition of a lattice.


1   Introduction
Lattices are discrete additive subgroups of Rm . A lattice is usually defined by a
set of n linearly independent basis vectors b1 , b2 , . . . , bn ∈ Rm , such that any
vector in the lattice can be expressed as an integer linear combination of the basis
vectors. Despite their simplicity, lattices offer a rich geometric structure that can
be used to define various computationally hard problems, the most important of
which are the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP), which involves finding the short-
est non-zero vector in a given lattice, and the Closest Vector Problem (CVP),
which involves finding the lattice point closest to a given target point. Both of
these problems are known to be NP-hard, and their theoretical complexity and
algorithms have been extensively studied [37,13,16,2,4]. A major challenge in
the area lies in comprehending the computational complexity of SVP, CVP and
related lattice problems for polynomial approximation factors, which constitute
the foundation of lattice-based cryptography.
    Apart from SVP and CVP, several other significant lattice-related problems
have gained significant interest. One such problem is the Lattice Isomorphism
Problem (LIP). Two lattices L1 and L2 are said to be isomorphic if there exists
an orthogonal transformation that maps L1 to L2 . The Decisional Lattice Iso-
morphism Problem (DLIP) is to decide whether there exists an orthogonal linear
transformation mapping L1 to L2 , and the Search Lattice Isomorphism Problem
(SLIP) is to find such an orthogonal transformation given two isomorphic lat-
tices L1 and L2 . In the formal definitions below, these lattices are represented
by integral Gram matrices, and an isomorphism is output as the corresponding
coordinate change matrix. Research on LIP can be traced back to the work of
Plesken and Souvignier [56,57], focusing on the creation of algorithms to address
low-dimensional instances of LIP. The asymptotic complexity of LIP was later
considered by Dutour Sikirić, Schürmann, and Vallentin [58]. They prove that
DLIP is at least as hard as the Graph Isomorphism Problem (GIP)3 . In [38], Haviv
and Regev propose an nO(n) -time algorithm for SLIP by using a new general-
ized isolation lemma [60] and an SVP oracle, which remains the fastest known
algorithm for solving SLIP, and they prove that DLIP ∈ SZK (statistical zero
knowledge). In [27], Sikirić et al. demonstrate that with access to an SVP ora-
cle, an SLIP instance can be reduced to a GIP instance. While GIP possesses a
quasi-polynomial time algorithm, as demonstrated in [10], the number of short-
est vectors within a lattice may be exponential in the worst case, potentially
resulting in an exponential-sized graph, as discussed in [27].
    Lattice Isomorphism Problems have recently been used to construct cryp-
tographic schemes, including public key encryption [15,1], fully-homomorphic
encryption [22,48], signature [25,26], key encapsulation mechanism [26], identi-
fication [26] and commitment schemes [41]. Most of these schemes are based on
lattice isomorphism problems with special algebraic (module-LIP) or geometric
properties (ZLIP), sparking renewed interest in the domain of lattice isomor-
phism problems. The module-LIP, an algebraic variant of LIP, was introduced
by Ducas et al. [25]. There is a series of cryptanalytic works on module-LIP
[53,50,8]. For ZLIP, the goal is to find an orthogonal transformation that maps
Zn to L, provided that L is isomorphic to Zn . Indeed, ZLIP is a well-known
problem, and determining its computational complexity has remained a long-
standing open question. This challenge has inspired a rich and elegant body of
research [34,59,31,43,44,47,40,18,15,42,24].
    Although both SLIP and DLIP are employed in various cryptographic schemes,
their computational complexity is not well understood, particularly compared
to the well-studied graph isomorphism problem (GIP). As mentioned above, all
existing algorithms for SLIP require the SVP oracle as a subroutine [38,27] and
in [38], Haviv and Regev prove that DLIP ∈ SZK, and it is well known that
SZK ⊆ AM ∩ coAM [30,5], thus DLIP is unlikely to be NP-hard, unless the poly-

    preserving bijection from the vertex set of G1 to that of G2 .

nomial hierarchy (PH) collapses [20]. Therefore, a natural question is whether
SLIP can be NP-hard, and in particular, is there a reduction from SVP to SLIP?
Careful readers may wonder whether there exists a reduction from SLIP to DLIP.
If such a reduction does exist, it would imply that SLIP is unlikely to be NP-
hard, unless PH collapses. However, our understanding of the reduction from
SLIP to DLIP remains limited. Currently, the only related works are [59,32]. In
[59], Szydlo established a polynomial-time reduction from the Search ZLIP prob-
lem to DLIP. In [32], van Gent and van Woerden extended this result to general
lattices with direct sum structures and modular lattices. In this respect, LIP is
different from GIP and Code Equivalence Problem 4 (CEP). For CEP, Petrank
and Roth show that it lies in NP ∩ coAM [55], Biasse and Micheli show that its
search version is polynomially equivalent to the decision version [17], thus the
search version of CEP is unlikely to be NP-hard. For GIP, it is shown in [35]
that GIP lies in NP ∩ coAM and the search version is polynomially equivalent to
the decision version [51]. In addition, it is shown in [51] that GIP, calculating a
set of generators of the automorphism group of a graph (GAP), counting all the
isomorphisms between the graphs (#GIP), calculating the order of the automor-
phism group of a graph (#GAP) are all polynomially equivalent. Similarly, we
can define these problems on lattice isomorphisms, but the reductions between
these problems are not well studied.
    Therefore, in this paper, we delve into the complexity of LIP and focus on
two key questions, namely,
Question 1. Is SLIP an NP-hard problem?

Question 2. What are the reductions among LAGP, SLIP, #LAP, and DLIP?

1.1    Our Results and Techniques
On Basing SLIP on NP-hardness
   For the first question, we provide a negative answer by proving that SLIP
cannot be NP-hard unless PH collapses. Specifically, we prove the following the-
orem:

Theorem 1.1 (see also Theorem 3.6). If there exists a randomized Turing
reduction from a decision problem L to SLIP, then L ∈ AM ∩ coAM.

   This result leads to the following interesting corollary, which uses the result
that SVP is NP-hard [6].
Corollary 1.2. If there exists a randomized Turing reduction from the shortest
vector problem SVP to SLIP, then NP ⊆ coAM.
   In order to obtain a black-box separation between SLIP and NP-hardness, let
R be a reduction from a decision problem L to SLIP. We aim to construct an

AM protocol for L using the reduction R. A natural approach is for the verifier
to sample a random tape and send it to the prover. The prover then simulates
the reduction R and answers any queries to SLIP by leveraging its unbounded
computational power. Subsequently, the prover sends the simulation transcript
along with the answers to the verifier, who checks their correctness. However,
since SLIP is a search problem, there is not always a unique correct answer. The
prover thus has the freedom to choose which answer to provide for each query.
This freedom enables a malicious prover to potentially deceive the verifier. This
issue can be addressed by shifting the search problem to a sampling problem,
since in this setting the correct answer distribution for each query is unique.
The idea was originally proposed by Bogdanov and Brzuska [19]. We adopt their
general proof framework, which mainly consists of two steps.
    The first step is to shift from a search problem to a sampling problem S.
The second step is to prove that this sampling problem possesses certain prop-
erties that can be leveraged to separate NP-hardness. In our proof, the sampling
problem S we use has a size-verifiable property.
    Inspired by [42], we defined a new sampling problem related to lattice auto-
morphisms, denoted as the Sampling Lattice Automorphism Problem (SaLAP):
                                                                                  $
on input an n-dimensional lattice L, SaLAP outputs a uniform sample φ ←
Aut(L).
    We then proved that there exists a randomized Turing reduction from SLIP to
SaLAP. A key technique in the reduction is a lemma concerning the structure of
the automorphism group of the direct sum of irreducible lattices. Informally, this
lemma states that for any automorphism ϕ on such a lattice, ϕ can be viewed as
a permutation of the irreducible lattice components. Here, an irreducible lattice
is defined as one that cannot be further orthogonally decomposed into two sub-
lattices. Moreover, each irreducible lattice plays a role analogous to a connected
component in a graph. In addition, according to the unique orthogonal decom-
position theorem proved by Eichler in 1952 [28], every lattice L has a unique
orthogonal decomposition L = N1 ⊕ · · · ⊕ Ns , where each Ni is an irreducible
lattice. 5
    Let us now outline the main idea. The reduction essentially follows a divide-
and-conquer approach. For an SLIP instance (L, L′ ), we first construct a lattice
N = L⊕L′ , and then aim to find a “lucky” automorphism in Aut(N ). From this
we can extract an isomorphism between L and L′ . However, the proportion of
such “lucky” automorphisms in the entire automorphism group depends on the
number of the irreducible components of L. When L is an irreducible lattice, we
can apply the aforementioned lemma to show that the proportion of “lucky” au-
tomorphisms in Aut(N ) is 1/2. If L has more irreducible components, then the
proportion of “lucky” automorphisms may be exponentially small. Fortunately,
if L is not an irreducible lattice, we can always use the uniform distribution on
Aut(N ) to orthogonally decompose L and L′ into L1 ⊕ L2 and L′1 ⊕ L′2 with
high probability, thereby reducing SLIP instance (L, L′ ) to two SLIP instances:

(L1 , L′1 ) and (L2 , L′2 ), where L1 and L2 have a smaller number of irreducible
components, thus obtaining a divide-and-conquer approach. Therefore, if a de-
cision problem L can be reduced to SLIP, then it can also be reduced to SaLAP.
    For the second step, we demonstrate that the size of the automorphism group
of a lattice is verifiable, meaning that the decision problem which, given a Gram
matrix G and an integer s, asks whether |Stab(G)| = s lies in AM. We actually
construct an IP protocol and then use the well-known results [36,11] to obtain
an AM protocol. The main techniques used in this protocol are the random-
ized self-reduction algorithm on LIP [26] and the BPP algorithm proposed by
Beals and Babai [12] for computing the order of finite subgroups on GLn (Q).
For a common input (G, s), the prover outputs a generating set {g1 , . . . , gk } of
Stab(G) and sends the set to the verifier. The verifier can use the randomized
self-reduction algorithm on LIP and the BPP algorithm proposed by Beals and
Babai to determine whether {g1 , . . . , gk } generates Stab(G), and then use the
algorithm of Beals and Babai to determine whether its order is equal to s.
    In the protocol, we represent lattices by Gram matrices; see Section 2 for the
common input model used throughout the paper.
    In addition, we reduce the computation of the orthogonal decomposition of
a lattice (LODP, see Definition 2.13) to calculating the Korkine-Zolotareff (KZ)
basis of a lattice.

Theorem 1.3 (see also Theorem 3.8). Let L be a full-rank lattice with a KZ
basis {b1 , b2 , . . . , bn }. Define a graph GL = (V, E) where V = {b1 , b2 , . . . , bn }
and (bi , bj ) ∈ E if and only if ⟨bi , bj ⟩ ≠ 0. Then, the unique orthogonal decom-
position is given by L = L1 ⊕ · · · ⊕ Ls , where each Li is spanned by the basis
vectors in the i-th connected component of GL , and is irreducible.

    It is a standard fact that KZ basis can be found using SVP oracle at most n
times. Thus, if we plug in the fastest known algorithm for SVP [3], we have the
following corollary.

Corollary 1.4. There is a randomized 2n+o(n) -time and space algorithm for
LODP.


The Reductions among LAGP, SLIP, #LAP, and DLIP
   For the second question, we have some positive answers. Specifically, we prove
that the reduction results on LIP correspond to most of the results on the GIP,
except for the reduction from #GAP to GIP and the reduction from Search GIP to
#GAP. These directions can be considered as open problems for future research.
   Our first reduction result corresponds to the reduction that GAP is a polynomial-
time equivalent to the search GIP, except that our reduction is a randomized
reduction.

Theorem 1.5 (see also Theorem 4.3). In the context of randomized Turing
reduction, LAGP is equivalent to SLIP.


                                            5
    This reduction uses a basic fact in computational group theory: computing
the generating set of a finite group is almost equivalent to uniform sampling
on this finite group [9,23]. Specifically, in [42], Jiang et al. use the randomized
self-reduction of LIP to prove that a reduction from SaLAP to SLIP. Combining
the reduction from SLIP to SaLAP we mentioned earlier, we can complete the
reduction. However, one thing to note is that when using a set of group generators
to uniformly sample group elements, there will be some errors in the distribution
(see Theorem 2.8). Therefore, we need to make a small modification to the
reduction proof from SLIP to SaLAP.
    From the above reduction and the algorithm of Beals and Babai [12] men-
tioned above, we can get the following reduction.

Corollary 1.6. There is a randomized Turing reduction from #LAP to SLIP.

  Combining this corollary with Theorem 1.1, we can obtain the result that
#LAP cannot be #P-complete unless PH collapses.
  Moreover, we demonstrate that there is an efficient reduction from DLIP to
#LAP.

Theorem 1.7 (see also Theorem 4.6). There is a Turing reduction from
DLIP to #LAP.

    Recall the reduction from GIP to #GAP, for a GIP instance (G1 , G2 ), we
can assume that G1 and G2 are connected graphs, because computing the con-
nected components of a graph is efficient. Then the reduction determines whether
G1 and G2 are isomorphic by analyzing the relationship among the quantities
#Aut(G1 ), #Aut(G2 ), and #Aut(G1 ⊕G2 ). For lattices, however, it is not known
whether the orthogonal decomposition of L can be computed efficiently, even
with access to a #LAP oracle. Interestingly, given a DLIP instance (L0 , L1 ), we
find that we can determine whether L0 is isomorphic to L1 by analyzing the
relationship among the quantities n00 = |Aut(L0 ⊕ L0 )|, n01 = |Aut(L0 ⊕ L1 )|,
and n11 = |Aut(L1 ⊕ L1 )|. Specifically, L0 is isomorphic to L1 if and only if
n00 = n01 = n11 holds. The proof of the reduction essentially relies on the
lemma concerning the structure of the automorphism group of the direct sum of
irreducible lattices that we mentioned earlier.
    Therefore, a direct corollary of the above theorem is that #LIP is polynomial-
time equivalent to #LAP, and we use similar reduction techniques to prove that
#LAP can be used to distinguish whether a lattice is irreducible.

Corollary 1.8. In the context of Turing reduction, #LIP is equivalent to #LAP.

      See Fig. 1 for a summary of our results.


1.2     Related Works

The potential of basing cryptography on the minimal assumption NP ̸⊆ BPP
lies at the core of complexity-theoretic cryptography. Previous investigations


                                         6
into constructing cryptography on worst-case NP-hardness have produced sev-
eral negative results for black-box reduction. The work of Akavia, Goldreich,
Goldwasser and Moshkovitz [7] and Bogdanov and Brzuska [19] showed that a
special class of one-way functions called size-verifiable one-way functions cannot
be based on NP-hardness. Liu [49] then generalized the proof framework in [19]
and proved that the search SIVPω(n log n) 6 is not NP-hard, unless PH collapses.
    Although we showed that SLIP is not NP-hard, an interesting result is that in
[14], Bennett, Dadush, and Stephens-Davidowitz introduced the Lattice Distor-
tion Problem (LDP), which serves as a generalization of LIP. LDP aims to deter-
mine the degree of “similarity” between two lattices: Given two n-dimensional
lattices L1 and L2 , the goal is to compute a bijective linear transformation T
that maps L1 to L2 while minimizing the condition number ∥T∥ · ∥T−1 ∥ of T,
where ∥T∥ = sup∥x∥=1 ∥Tx∥. They showed that LDP is NP-hard to approximate
to within any constant factor (under randomized reductions), by a reduction
from SVP.
    In [39], Hemkemeier and Vallentin presented an algorithm based on Kneser’s
method to solve the Lattice Orthogonal Decomposition Problem (LODP, see
Definition 2.13). Given a generating system S = {v1 , . . . , vs } = {v ∈ L : ∥v∥ ≤
B} for an n-dimensional lattice L, s = |S|, their algorithm solves the LODP
in O(n6 log2 B + sn2 ) time. However, their analysis does not account for the
complexity of constructing this set S. This pre-computation can be a significant
bottleneck, as the number of vectors s can be exponentially large. In fact, the
parameter B needs to be at least larger than λn . Thus, the time complexity of
precomputing this part is at least 2n+o(n) , since it requires solving at least one
instance of SVP.

definitions and preliminaries. In Section 3, we prove our main result and its
corollary. In Section 4, we show the reduction results corresponding to the known
results in the graph isomorphism problem.

2.3   Lattice Isomorphism and Automorphism
The automorphism group Aut(L) of an n-dimensional lattice L consists of all
orthogonal matrices that preserve L, i.e.,
                       Aut(L) = {φ ∈ On (R) : φ(L) = L}.
It is clear that Aut(L) contains the automorphisms ±In , called trivial automor-
phisms of L.
    The set of isomorphisms Iso(L1 , L2 ) between two n-dimensional lattices L1 , L2
consists of all orthogonal matrices that send L1 to L2 , i.e.,
                    Iso(L1 , L2 ) = {φ ∈ On (R) : φ(L1 ) = L2 }.
If Iso(L1 , L2 ) ̸= ∅, take an arbitrary element φ ∈ Iso(L1 , L2 ). It is straight-

a coset of Aut(L1 ) in On (R). Two lattices are said to be isomorphic, written

5   Conclusion
In this paper, we demonstrate that SLIP cannot be NP-hard unless PH col-
lapses, by leveraging the randomized self-reduction algorithm of LIP together
with the properties of irreducible lattices. Furthermore, we reduce the task of
computing the orthogonal decomposition of a lattice to that of calculating the
KZ basis, thereby revealing a novel structural connection between KZ bases and
irreducible decompositions. Additionally, we establish reductions among LAGP,
SLIP, #LAP, #LIP, and DLIP, thereby deepening our understanding of the com-
plexity landscape surrounding LIP.
     As a direction for future research, it remains an intriguing open problem
whether a reduction exists from SLIP to #LAP and from #LAP to DLIP. More-
over, investigating whether such reductions could be exploited to design a more
efficient algorithm for SLIP represents another important avenue for exploration.
